# Control Your DAW with the Roland MC-500mkII

> **Stage:** Outlining — this document is the outline. On approve, it gets snapshotted to `scrapbook/outline.md` and `index.md` gets rewritten as the draft body.

**Demo video:** https://youtu.be/IIhBlliWr9k — payoff moment in §05 ("The moment it works").

## Frame

The dispatch is *not* about the implementation. The implementation is a callout. The dispatch is about a small mission-aligned thing: two great things on the shelf — the Roland MC-500mkII and your DAW — that couldn't talk, and now they can. That's what audiocontrol is for. Modern tooling for great vintage gear so the hardware doesn't have to retire just because the software around it moved on.

## Dek (one sentence)

Two great things that couldn't talk, finally talking. The Roland MC-500mkII (1988) drives your DAW's transport, jog, and 99 locate memories via a small bridge service — turning thirty-year-old hardware into a tactile controller for whatever you're recording today.

*(Alt deks to consider:)*
- "The MC-500mkII has the best transport buttons in your studio. Your DAW has the takes. A small bridge makes them work as one."
- "Modern tooling for great vintage gear: the MC-500mkII (1988) becomes an MCU controller for any DAW that speaks Mackie."

## Section structure

Seven sections. Magazine dividers (`---`) between in the rendered article. Sentence-case headings. Narrative arc: dissonance → desire → bridge → payoff → mission. Implementation lives in **one callout** under §03, not as its own section.

### § 01 — Two great things that couldn't talk

Open with the dissonance plainly. *I've got a DAW. I've got a Roland MC-500mkII. They both do their job beautifully — and they don't talk.*

State what each one is good at, in one paragraph each:

- **The MC-500mkII.** 1988. 8-track multitrack recorder for MIDI. Built like flight hardware. The best transport buttons in the studio: real travel, real feel, designed for hours of takes. Speaks 1988-era MIDI — SPP, transport, 99 location memories.
- **The DAW.** Whichever modern DAW you live in. Logic, Ableton Live, LUNA. Speaks MCU when you give it an MCU controller. Doesn't natively understand any of the MC-500's MIDI.

End the section: I want to hit play on the MC-500 and have the DAW play. That should be possible. It isn't, by default.

### § 02 — The desire

Why this matters, briefly. The hardware sequencer was designed for an era when the studio's tape machine was the master. The DAW replaced the tape machine, but the sequencer's transport language stayed in 1988. The buttons are still the best buttons. The wheel is still the best wheel. The only thing missing is the wire from those controls into the modern session.

This is what audiocontrol is for, in one sentence. Modern tooling for great vintage gear so the hardware on your shelf doesn't have to retire just because the software around it moved on.

### § 03 — The bridge (with implementation in a callout)

A small service that runs on your laptop. Listens to the MC-500mkII over MIDI. Speaks MCU to your DAW. The MC-500mkII's panel becomes a tactile transport controller for the modern session.

ASCII diagram:

```
MC-500mkII  →  bridge  →  MCU  →  DAW
   (MIDI)              (CoreMIDI virtual port)
```

Implementation callout (3–4 sentences max — operator's note: don't make this the article):

> **How it works, briefly.** The bridge converts the MC-500's MIDI Song Position Pointer into MTC at the DAW's session sample rate, wraps it in MCU `LOCATE`, and lets the DAW seek. Transport (start/stop/continue) maps directly to MCU transport. The jog wheel becomes MCU jog deltas scaled to the DAW's frame rate. No driver, no kernel extension, no DAW plugin — the bridge exposes a CoreMIDI virtual port the DAW connects to as a standard MCU surface.

### § 04 — What you actually get

The MC-500mkII's panel mapped to the DAW transport one-for-one. Stop, play, record, fast-forward, rewind. The data wheel becomes the jog wheel — fine resolution slow, faster scrub when you spin.

The interesting part is the location memories. The MC-500mkII stores 99 location markers in NVRAM. Pre-configure verse / chorus / bridge as MC-500 locations; one button on the panel jumps the DAW to that bar and beat. The MC-500's panel becomes a tactile arrangement-jumping interface for whatever DAW is on the other end. Years of muscle memory finally pay rent.

### § 05 — The moment it works (demo video)

Embed: <https://youtu.be/IIhBlliWr9k>

The MC-500mkII driving LUNA's transport. Hit play on the MC-500, LUNA plays. Spin the wheel, LUNA jogs. Recall a location, LUNA seeks. The dispatch's payoff lives here — the reader has been promised a thing that works; here is the thing working. Don't over-narrate the video; one paragraph above the embed setting the scene, and trust the reader to watch.

This is also where the VO from the recording session lives: *"hit play on the MC-500, and you get the transport, which I think is pretty great."* (Quote inline.)

### § 06 — What's tested

Three bolded lead-ins. Audiocontrol's signature "honest about limits" register:

- **Hardware.** Roland MC-500mkII · 1988 · 8-track · Super MRC OS. The Super MRC OS is the load-bearing requirement — the original 1986 MC-500 lacks it. The Roland MC-50 (1989, smaller, similar architecture) probably works, untested.
- **DAWs.** Logic Pro, Ableton Live, LUNA. MCU is a standard; in theory any DAW that accepts an MCU controller should work. I'm only claiming the three I've run end-to-end.
- **Platform.** macOS via CoreMIDI. The Linux build uses ALSA virtual ports; that path compiles and runs but I haven't put it against a real DAW. No Windows build yet.

### § 07 — Get it / what's next

The bridge ships from `audiocontrol-org/audiocontrol` releases:

- Pre-compiled binaries for macOS and Linux
- Homebrew formula
- macOS `.app` — drag into `/Applications/`. No terminal required.

→ Releases: <https://github.com/audiocontrol-org/audiocontrol/releases>
→ Source: <https://github.com/audiocontrol-org/audiocontrol>

What's next, briefly: MC-50 verification. Windows. More MCU surface (channel select, v-pots) when something on the bench needs it.

If you have an MC-500mkII and a DAW, try it. If it breaks on your setup, file an issue with the platform and DAW version.
